The Atlantic petrel (Pterodroma incerta) is a large gadfly petrel that breeds in dense colonies on remote subantarctic islands. Field studies on Gough Island have documented the species' developmental biology in detail. Eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and hatch after an average of 55.5 days [ab = 55.5 days], an extended incubation period typical of procellariiform seabirds. The newly hatched chicks, or downy nestlings, weigh approximately 70 grams [Wwb = approximately 70 grams] upon hatching, a modest initial body mass that reflects the considerable yolk investment required to sustain the embryo through the protracted incubation. This neonatal mass is comparable to values reported for other large Pterodroma species, such as Pterodroma macroptera, and represents a key starting point for the subsequent rapid somatic growth phase that characterises the nestling period.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), the developmental trajectory of the nestling proceeds through predictable milestones. The chick attains sustained flight and fledges at 138 days after hatching [tx = 138 days after hatching], a duration that aligns with the extended post-hatching development documented among gadfly petrels at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. During this period of parental-fed growth, the nestling undergoes a remarkable transformation in body mass, accumulating tissue until it reaches an asymptotic ultimate wet weight of 750 grams [Wwi = 750 grams] prior to fledging. This adult-sized mass, which is among the highest recorded for the genus, is achieved through the efficient conversion of lipid-rich stomach oil provisions delivered by both parents, a metabolic feat that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to rear a single offspring in the nutrient-poor Southern Ocean. The fledging age of approximately 4.5 months reflects the time required to complete feather development and deposit sufficient energy reserves for the challenging post-fledging period of independence.

Sexual maturity in this species is attained relatively late compared to other seabirds of equivalent body mass. Under the typical thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], juvenile birds that survive the post-fledging period of high mortality undergo gonadal maturation by approximately 414 days since birth [tp = approximately 414 days since birth]. This prolonged period of physiological immaturity, which is consistent with the delayed reproductive schedules observed across the family Procellariidae, likely stems from the considerable challenges young petrels face in mastering the foraging skills necessary to secure sufficient prey in the pelagic environment. The protracted sub-adult phase allows individuals to acquire the body condition and social experience required before they can successfully incubate an egg and provision a rapidly growing chick.

First reproduction occurs even later than the onset of puberty, with individuals typically initiating their first breeding attempt at 730 days since birth [tR = 730 days since birth] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This deferral of reproductive effort is a common feature among long-lived seabirds, reflecting the time needed to attain the nesting experience and body condition necessary for successful chick rearing. The Atlantic petrel, like many of its congeners, lays a single egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = single egg per breeding attempt] and, at most, raises one chick per year [Ri = one chick per year]. This extremely low annual reproductive output is at the extreme end of the range for the genus and represents a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival and iteroparity over a long lifetime rather than high immediate fecundity.

The Atlantic petrel exemplifies an extreme K-selected life-history strategy, with adults exhibiting remarkable longevity. Maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years], a duration that places this species among the longest-lived of the procellariiform seabirds at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, sustained at a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], allows individuals to accumulate numerous reproductive events over many decades despite the high per-capita energetic cost of each single-chick brood. The sustained high adult survival rates that accompany such longevity are essential for maintaining population stability, and field studies on Gough Island have noted that annual mortality rates remain exceptionally low in the absence of introduced predators, with breeding individuals frequently returning to the same burrow site for more than two decades.
